title: Statistics: Regression and Correlation
summary: Bivariate data, scatter plots, the least-squares regression line, the correlation coefficient $r$, and making and judging predictions.

notes.text: **Bivariate data** has two variables for each item, such as hours studied ($x$) and test mark ($y$). A **scatter plot** shows each pair as a point, revealing any relationship.

rows: Points rise from left to right
Positive correlation: as $x$ increases, $y$ tends to increase
Points fall from left to right

notes.caption: The line of best fit: $b$ is the gradient and $a$ the $y$-intercept (found on the calculator in STAT mode, linear regression)

notes.text: The least-squares line minimises the sum of the squared vertical distances from the points to the line. It always passes through the point $(\bar{x}; \bar{y})$.
The **correlation coefficient** $r$ measures the strength and direction of a **linear** relationship, with $-1 \leq r \leq 1$.

notes.title: Worked example 1
notes.problem: Hours studied: 1; 2; 3; 4; 5; 6. Marks: 45; 50; 58; 62; 70; 77. Find the regression line and $r$, and predict the mark for 7 hours.

notes.label: Interpolation and extrapolation
notes.text: Predictions **within** the range of the data (interpolation) are more reliable than predictions **outside** it (extrapolation). Predicting a mark for 20 hours of study would give over 160%, which is impossible.

notes.label: Correlation is not causation
notes.text: A strong correlation does not prove that one variable causes the other. Ice-cream sales and drownings are correlated because both increase in hot weather.

notes.title: Interpreting $r$
notes.problem: For hours watching TV and test marks, $r = -0{,}87$. Interpret this.
steps: The negative sign: as one increases, the other decreases.
A value close to $-1$ means a strong relationship.
notes.answer: A strong negative correlation. It does not prove that TV causes lower marks.

questions.prompt: In a scatter plot the points fall from left to right. The correlation is…
Which value cannot be a correlation coefficient?
The regression line is $\hat{y} = 12 + 3{,}5x$. Predict $y$ when $x = 8$.
The least-squares regression line always passes through $(\bar{x}; \bar{y})$.
Data: $x$: 2; 4; 6; 8; 10 and $y$: 5; 9; 12; 17; 20. Use a calculator to find the equation of the least-squares regression line and the correlation coefficient.
Why is it risky to use a regression line to make predictions far outside the range of the data?
questions.memo:
✓ The relationship may not continue in the same way beyond the data (1)
✓ so predictions may be unrealistic or impossible (1)

questions.prompt: A study finds a strong positive correlation between shoe size and reading ability in primary school children. Does a bigger foot cause better reading? Explain.
questions.memo:
✓ No (1)
✓ Both increase with age (a third variable); correlation does not prove causation (1)

questions.prompt: Interpret the gradient $b = 6{,}4$ in worked example 1.
questions.memo:
✓ For each extra hour of study (1)
✓ the mark increases by about 6,4% on average (1)

questions.prompt: What does a correlation coefficient of $r = 0{,}2$ tell you about predictions made with the regression line?
questions.memo:
✓ The linear correlation is weak (1)
✓ so predictions will not be reliable (1)
